name: Isaiah
v: Listen to me, you who chase after righteousness, you who hunt for the LORD. Look at the rock you were cut from, the quarry you were dug out of.
Look at Abraham, your father. Look at Sarah, who bore you. He was one man when I called him — and I blessed him, and I multiplied him.

So the LORD will comfort Zion. He will comfort every ruin of her. He will turn her wilderness into Eden, her desert into the garden of the LORD. Joy and gladness will be found there — thanksgiving, and the sound of singing.
Pay attention to me, my people. Listen, my nation. Instruction will go out from me, and my justice — I will set it up as a light for the peoples.
My righteousness is on its way. My salvation has gone out. My arms will judge the nations. The coastlands wait for me. They put their hope in my arm.

Lift your eyes to the sky. Look at the earth beneath you. The heavens will dissolve like smoke. The earth will wear out like a garment. Its inhabitants will die like gnats. But my salvation will stand forever. My righteousness will not break.
Listen to me, you who know what righteousness is — you, the people with my instruction written on your heart. Do not fear the contempt of mortals. Do not crumble at their insults.
The moth will eat them like wool. The worm will devour them like cloth. But my righteousness stands forever. My salvation runs through every generation.
Wake up! Wake up! Put on your strength, arm of the LORD! Wake up like the old days, like the generations long gone. Were you not the arm that hacked Rahab to pieces, that ran the dragon through?
Were you not the arm that dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep — that carved a road through the seabed for the redeemed to cross?

The ransomed of the LORD will come home. They will enter Zion singing. Joy will crown their heads — joy that never ends. Gladness and joy will overtake them. Sorrow and sighing will run for their lives.
I am the one who comforts you. I am. So who are you, that you should be afraid of a mortal who dies — of a human being who is grass?

You have forgotten the LORD who made you, who stretched out the heavens, who laid the foundations of the earth. And every day, all day, you tremble at the fury of the oppressor as he sets himself to destroy. But where is the fury of the oppressor now?
The prisoner bent low will soon be released. He will not die in the pit. His bread will not run out.
I am the LORD your God — the one who churns the sea so its waves roar. The LORD of Armies is my name.
I have put my words in your mouth. I have hidden you in the shadow of my hand — I, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth, who say to Zion: You are my people.
Wake up! Wake up! Get on your feet, Jerusalem — you who have drunk from the LORD's hand the cup of his fury, who have drained the goblet of staggering down to the dregs.
Of all the sons she bore, not one to guide her. Of all the sons she raised, not one to take her by the hand.
Two disasters have struck you — who will grieve for you? Devastation and destruction. Famine and sword. Who will comfort you?
Your sons lie unconscious at every street corner, like antelope tangled in a net — full to the brim with the fury of the LORD, with the rebuke of your God.
So listen to this, you afflicted one — drunk, but not from wine.
This is what your Lord says — the LORD your God, who fights for his people: Look. I am taking the cup of staggering out of your hand. The goblet of my fury — you will never drink from it again.
I am putting it into the hand of those who tormented you — those who said to you, Bow down so we can walk over you. And you made your back the ground. You made yourself the street they walked on.

com.d:
# Isaiah 51: The Comfort of God's Eternal Strength

At its heart, Isaiah 51 invites God's weary people to find their identity and hope not in their present circumstances, but in the eternal character and strength of their Creator. Through poetic imagery and direct address, the prophet calls Israel to remember who they are and whose they are, even in the midst of exile and suffering.

The passage opens with an invitation to "look to the rock from which you were hewn"—a call to remember Abraham and Sarah, the foundational ancestors of faith. Isaiah uses this genealogical anchor to remind the people that God has a pattern of bringing life from impossible situations. What once seemed barren and hopeless became fruitful, and that same creative power remains available. The prophet speaks as if comfort is already present, not merely promised for some distant future. "The Lord will surely comfort Zion," he declares, assuring listeners that consolation is not contingent but certain.

This message speaks powerfully to our modern experience of depletion and discouragement. We live in seasons when our strength fails, when circumstances press us beyond our confidence, when the future looks uncertain. Isaiah reminds us that our sufficiency lies elsewhere—in a God whose compassion endures and whose salvation is everlasting. Notice that God's comfort comes not through removing difficulty but through renewing our inner fortitude and reconnecting us to His purposes.

The prophet also emphasizes the temporary nature of suffering: "Your sorrow will be forgotten, and your mourning will be gone." This does not dismiss real pain but contextualizes it within God's larger narrative of restoration. When we align ourselves with His eternal purposes rather than our temporary trials, perspective shifts. Our trials become temporary; His faithfulness becomes permanent.

As you sit with this passage, ask yourself: Where have I forgotten my identity as God's beloved? What ancestral faith or testimony can remind me that He has always been faithful? How might I embrace comfort not as the absence of struggle but as the presence of His sustaining power?
com.s:
Isaiah 51 stands as a magnificent oracle of consolation situated within the larger corpus commonly designated Deutero-Isaiah (chapters 40–55), composed during the Babylonian exile around 540 BCE as the Persian king Cyrus was ascending to power. The prophet addresses a despairing community of Judean exiles, summoning them to renewed faith through a sophisticated interweaving of creation theology, ancestral traditions, and eschatological hope.

The chapter opens with a threefold summons using the imperative "listen" or "hearken" (שִׁמְעוּ, *shim'u*), structuring the discourse into distinct yet interconnected units. This rhetorical device draws the faithful remnant—described as those who "pursue righteousness" and "seek the LORD"—into attentive reception of divine comfort. The invocation of Abraham and Sarah as the paradigmatic ancestors carries profound theological weight; just as God blessed and multiplied one couple, so too will the diminished exilic community experience divine fecundation and restoration.

Central to the passage is the term "comfort" or "consolation" (נֶחָמָה, *neḥamah*), which echoes the programmatic declaration of Isaiah 40:1 and establishes the dominant tenor of this prophetic collection. The divine promise transforms Zion's wilderness into Eden, her desert into the garden of the LORD—imagery deliberately evoking primordial creation while anticipating new creation. This theological move situates Israel's historical restoration within cosmic dimensions.

The concept of divine "arm" (זְרוֹעַ, *zeroa'*) appears prominently, personified as the instrument of salvation that once defeated the primordial chaos monster Rahab and dried up the sea—mythological language applied to the Exodus event. This conflation of creation mythology with salvation history demonstrates the prophet's sophisticated theological synthesis, suggesting that redemption constitutes nothing less than re-creation.

Scholarly debate surrounds the relationship between verses 9–11, which some consider a later liturgical interpolation due to their hymnic quality and the community's responsive voice. The passage's canonical placement proves significant, as it anticipates the Suffering Servant poem of chapter 53 while echoing themes from earlier Isaianic traditions, thus contributing to the book's complex literary unity despite its compositional diversity.
com.p:
Isaiah 51 emerges from the prophet's pen around 700 years before the incarnation of Christ, yet it speaks with the voice of one who has already seen Babylon's fall and Israel's restoration—testimony to the Spirit's sovereign authorship across time. Within the grand redemptive arc, this chapter stands at the threshold between Exile and Restoration, offering comfort to a people who would not taste Babylonian captivity for another century yet, while simultaneously reaching forward to realities that extend through the Cross, into the Church Age, and onward to the New Creation.

The chapter opens with a summons to "look to the rock from which you were hewn," directing Israel's gaze backward to Abraham and Sarah. This is no mere historical reminiscence but typological instruction: as God called one barren couple and multiplied them into a nation, so He will transform Zion's waste places into Eden-like gardens. Abraham thus stands as a type of the new humanity God creates from spiritual barrenness, a pattern fulfilled ultimately in Christ, the true Seed through whom all nations receive blessing.

Three times the divine voice commands attention—"Listen to me"—unveiling layers of prophetic promise. The law going forth from Zion and justice becoming a light to the peoples finds initial fulfillment in Christ's teaching ministry and the apostolic proclamation, yet presses toward that final Day when righteousness covers the earth as waters cover the sea. The heavens vanishing like smoke and the earth wearing out like a garment echo the eschatological renovation Peter describes, when the elements dissolve and new heavens and new earth emerge.

The "cup of staggering" passage reveals profound typological depth. Jerusalem drank divine wrath to its dregs, yet this cup was lifted from her lips and placed into the hands of her tormentors. Christ entered this mystery most fully in Gethsemane, drinking the cup of God's fury so that His people might receive instead the cup of blessing. What Israel experienced partially in her restoration from Babylon, the Church inherits fully through the Cross.

The triumphant cry "Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD" finds its answer in the resurrection—God's arm made bare before all nations. For the Church dwelling between the advents, Isaiah 51 declares that the same creative power that divided the sea and ransomed Israel has conquered death itself, guaranteeing that every exile ends, every waste place blooms, and everlasting joy crowns every pilgrim reaching Zion.
